idiom_name: bounded queue + worker pool + explicit full-policy
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: place a bounded FIFO between producers and consumers; producers enqueue according to a declared full-policy (block, reject, drop or dead-letter) and a fixed set of consumers takes-and-acknowledges, processing at their own pace. The bound is the latency and memory budget, not a tuning afterthought, and it is the reason the pattern levels load instead of deferring a crash. Make the consumer loop the only place that touches the service, attach retry/backoff, idempotency and dead-lettering at the queue, and move the queue out of process (broker) when accepted work must survive restarts or be shared by several hosts. Where the platform already ships a bounded blocking queue or channel, use it instead of writing one.
code_sketch:
queue = bounded_fifo(capacity=N)          # the bound = the leveling budget
producer:
    enqueue(item)                        # waits / rejects / drops per policy
consumer (x W workers):
    loop: item = queue.take()            # waits while empty
          try: process(item); ack(item)
          except: retry(item) or dead_letter(item)
monitor: queue.depth, queue.oldest_age      # alert on age, not only throughput
pitfalls: An unbounded buffer is not load leveling; it merely postpones the failure to a memory or broker-quota exhaustion.
Missing acknowledgement or idempotency turns at-least-once delivery into duplicated work.
Queue depth is the control signal for scaling; without monitoring, a growing backlog is a silent outage.
Batching matters: one message per tiny unit multiplies broker overhead and defeats throughput.

Wrong move: let an unbounded queue or retention window absorb every overload -> storage fills and queue age becomes an unbounded latency debt -> bound capacity/retention and choose an explicit reject, shed, or dead-letter policy.

Wrong move: autoscale consumers solely from queue depth -> aggregate calls overwhelm the downstream service and trigger throttling/retry storms -> cap total concurrency/rate at the dependency and scale only within that budget.

Wrong move: acknowledge before the side effect is durable or assume one delivery -> crashes lose accepted work or retries duplicate it -> acknowledge after success, make writes idempotent, and route poison messages to a dead-letter queue.
